notes: Characters hold their looks, and the camera stops turning every shot into a selfie. Three things were working against identity. The written appearance anchor — which image models follow far harder than they follow reference photos — only rode selfies, so every ordinary photo a character appeared in was painted with no description of them at all, which is why they drifted worst on tame pictures. The anchor also led the prompt, and opening with a face description asks for a face-forward portrait; a first-person shot of someone's own feet came back framed like a mirror selfie. And on the reference-photo path every LoRA was weakened to keep style from overpowering identity, including the likeness LoRA that was the identity. Now the director reports whether the character is actually in frame, the anchor rides any picture they are in, the scene keeps the opening position so the camera survives, and likeness LoRAs are left at full strength. Their appearance is also an editable field on the character at last: it was learned once from a reference photo and then frozen out of sight, and it is the single strongest control over whether they look like themselves.
